chunks: "I define the inductor current flowing left to right, from the switch node to the output, and the voltage positive at the switch-node end when it's pushing that current up.
In the on state the high-side FET ties the switch node to the input. The output is at 3. 3 volts, so the switch-node side of the inductor is at 12 volts and the output side at 3.
7 volts on the switch-node end, which is positive across the inductor in the direction of the current, so the current ramps up and the inductor is absorbing energy.
In the off state the high-side FET opens, but the inductor current can't stop.
Its voltage flips: it tries to keep the current going, and the switch node swings down until the diode or low-side FET conducts and clamps it at about zero.
Now the output side is at 3. 3 volts and the switch-node side is at zero or slightly below, so the polarity is reversed: negative 3.
3 volts on the switch-node end relative to the output. The current is still flowing the same way, but now it's falling and the inductor is giving energy to the output.
So the polarity flips every cycle between plus V in-V out and minus V out , with the two areas equal in steady state."
